title: Endoreversible Carnot machines with long-time reversible limit
abstract: The well-known Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) engine [Am. J. Phys. {\bf 43}, 22 (1975)] runs in finite time and yields a finite power output. In order to recover the standard Carnot cycle from the CA model, the limit of quasi-static operation has to be concurrent with the reversible limit, a condition strangely missing from the CA model. We augment this model by specifying the duration of the isothermal process as a monotonic decreasing function of the temperature difference between the working substance and the reservoir. As an illustration, we analyze the machine's operation in the low-dissipation regime in which the entropy production in each isothermal branch is inversely proportional to the duration of the process. The modified model is able to determine the optimal durations of isothermal processes as well as heat and work per cycle, while retaining the optimal power conditions of the CA model.
summary: This paper improves upon the Curzon-Ahlborn model for heat engines by incorporating a specific dependence of process duration on temperature differences. This modification allows the calculation of absolute energy and time scales, successfully recovering the reversible Carnot limit while optimizing the power output across different operational regimes.
main_problem: To augment the Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) model for endoreversible Carnot machines to recover the standard Carnot cycle limit while determining absolute time and energy scales.
main_result: The modified model successfully determines absolute time and energy scales, showing that maximum power is achieved at an intermediate efficiency value corresponding to the CA model's optimal point.
method: The analysis augments the CA model by specifying a relationship between isothermal process duration and temperature difference, utilizing the low-dissipation regime assumption for entropy production ($S_{ir} \propto 1/t$).
model_or_system: The system is an endoreversible Carnot engine operating between hot and cold reservoirs. The model incorporates finite-time thermodynamics where irreversibility occurs during heat exchange with the environment.
key_observables: Efficiency ($\eta$), Work output per cycle ($W$), Maximum Power ($P_{max}$), Optimal temperature ratios ($	au^*$).
important_parameters: Temperature difference, process duration ($	au$), dissipation parameters ($\kappa, \sigma, 	heta$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is relating process duration ($t$) and temperature difference ($\delta T$) to ensure recovery of the reversible limit in the quasi-static limit; it also uses a low-dissipation approximation.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes, but the analysis involves deriving optimal parameters for power vs. efficiency trade-offs.
paper_structure: The paper first addresses the limitations of the CA model and then introduces an augmentation based on process duration dependence. It analyzes performance metrics (efficiency, work) under this modified framework, culminating in optimization procedures for maximum power output.
why_interesting: While focused on classical thermodynamics, the rigorous treatment of finite-time processes and approaching reversible limits shares conceptual links with non-equilibrium quantum dynamics where time scales are crucial.
